title: Truth Social Scandal: Selling Government Information for Profit
description_short: Truth Social Scandal: Selling Government Information for Profit
description_medium: The Intercept Media and Freedom of the Press Foundation sued in federal court in Manhattan over Truth Social’s paid Truth API, which they allege gives subscribers faster access to Trump’s official announcements. Their August 2026 complaint says subscriptions cost up to $100,000 a month and claims the practice violates the First and Fifth Amendments.
description_long: The Intercept Media and Freedom of the Press Foundation filed a complaint on August 12, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, docket 1:26-cv-06867. They sued Donald Trump in his official capacity, White House aides Natalie Harp and Daniel Scavino, the Executive Office of the President, and the White House Office. The complaint alleges that government announcements are posted on Truth Social before paid Truth API customers receive them at higher speed, while free access is delayed. It says the service costs up to $100,000 a month, or $60,000 a month with a three-year commitment, and argues that the arrangement gives wealthy subscribers preferential access to public information. The plaintiffs claim violations of the First and Fifth Amendments and seek declaratory and injunctive relief. Those are allegations in a filed complaint, not findings by a court. The low-quality linked article did not load in the source reader; the federal complaint itself and CNN’s contemporaneous report supply the identifiable case and terms.

title: The Last Trump Elections
description_short: The outcome of the next election will not change regardless of what Trump says or does. Trump has consistently claimed that the American Left steals elections at his expense.
description_medium: In an August 2026 opinion piece, Ian Bremmer predicts that Democrats are likely to win the House and may win the Senate in November’s midterms. He argues Trump will reject unfavorable results but cannot change state-administered outcomes, which courts and even Republicans will ultimately accept.
description_long: Ian Bremmer’s August 16, 2026, EL PAÍS opinion piece forecasts how Donald Trump and the parties may respond to that November’s midterm elections. Bremmer expects Democrats to win the House and says the Senate is a closer contest. He predicts that Trump will challenge unfavorable results, including by questioning voting machines and election workers, while state officials conduct the count. The article argues that the president cannot determine election outcomes because administration belongs to the states; it expects courts to reject post-election challenges and Republican officials to proceed with the next political cycle. Bremmer supports his forecast with Trump’s claims about the 2016, 2020, and 2024 elections, his pressure on Republican candidates and congressional leaders, and his current low polling. These are the author’s judgments about a future election, not findings about how the 2026 vote will turn out. The linked piece does not claim that Trump’s statements have no effect on political debate; it predicts that they will not alter the certified outcome.

preserved_fields.title: The Last Trump Elections
preserved_fields.description_short: The outcome of the next election will not change regardless of what Trump says or does. Trump has consistently claimed that the American Left steals elections at his expense.

notes: The complete EL PAÍS opinion piece discusses the November 2026 congressional midterms, forecasts a likely Democratic House win and a closer Senate race, and predicts Trump will challenge an unfavorable result but not change certified outcomes. Its forecast is opinion, not a verified outcome.

title: Whistleblower Says Trump Officials Predetermined Conclusions in Harvard Antisemitism Probe
description_short: Whistleblower Says Trump Officials Predetermined Conclusions in Harvard Antisemitism Probe
description_medium: A whistleblower has come forward alleging that Trump officials predetermined the conclusions of an investigation into antisemitism at Harvard. The investigation was launched after allegations of antisemitic incidents on campus. The whistleblower's claims suggest that the investigation was politicized and that the conclusions were predetermined.
description_long: The Harvard Crimson reported that Haley Van Erem, a former Justice Department civil rights attorney, filed a 25-page whistleblower disclosure alleging that Trump administration officials predetermined university antisemitism investigations and considered broad penalties before establishing Title VI violations. The filing described proposed Harvard settlement terms, including police memorandums and other reforms that Van Erem said raised First Amendment concerns. The disclosure went to the Office of Special Counsel and inspector general offices at DOJ and HHS and was shared with congressional judiciary committees. The Crimson recounts an alleged conversation with HHS Acting General Counsel Sean Keveney about Harvard being “over a barrel,” and reports that the DOJ said it stood behind the investigations’ integrity and that Van Erem was not assigned to them. The article presents the whistleblower’s allegations and the department’s response; it does not establish that investigators or a court substantiated them. It also does not report whether the offices opened investigations into her disclosure or what findings they reached. Those review outcomes remain unknown from this source.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

title: Pardons Robert Zangrillo
description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to Robert Zangrillo as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: The Justice Department lists a full pardon for Robert Zangrillo on January 19, 2021, while showing no sentence. AP reported that he had pleaded not guilty in the Varsity Blues college-admissions case and was awaiting trial. The sources do not explain Trump’s reason for granting the pardon.
description_long: The Justice Department’s clemency list places Robert Zangrillo’s full pardon on January 19, 2021, and records no sentence. The entry lists charges in the District of Massachusetts, including conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud, honest-services fraud, federal-program bribery, and money laundering. Associated Press reporting says prosecutors alleged Zangrillo paid $250,000 to secure his daughter’s transfer admission to the University of Southern California; he pleaded not guilty and was scheduled for trial in September 2021. The timing indicates that the pardon came before trial, rather than after a sentence. The pardon record does not state why Trump granted it, and the White House material reviewed here offers no person-specific explanation. The case allegations should not be treated as a conviction. The available documents establish the pardon date, listed charges, and the reported pending case, but an official explanation for the decision is still missing.

title: Pardons Weldon Angelos
description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to Weldon Angelos as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump granted Weldon Angelos a full pardon on December 22, 2020. The White House said Angelos had served 13 years of a 55-year sentence for marijuana sales and firearm offenses, and highlighted his criminal-justice reform advocacy, support from elected officials, and broader calls for second chances.
description_long: The White House announced a full pardon for Weldon Angelos on December 22, 2020. It said he had been sentenced in 2002 to 55 years for selling marijuana and carrying a handgun during a drug deal; the judge had described the mandatory-minimum sentence as unjust and irrational. Angelos was released by court order after serving 13 years, before Trump’s pardon. The White House statement emphasized his later criminal-justice reform advocacy and support from Senators Mike Lee and Rand Paul, Alice Johnson, and former U.S. Attorney Brett Tolman. The pardon removed the federal conviction’s remaining legal consequences; it did not cause his earlier release from prison. The available clemency statement presents advocacy and second chances as the administration’s rationale. The DOJ warrant identifies the District of Utah case, docket 2:02-cr-00708-001, and the pardon itself. This account distinguishes the earlier court-ordered release from the later presidential pardon.

title: Pardons Tommaso Buti
description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to Tommaso Buti as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: The DOJ pardon list records a full pardon for Tommaso Buti on January 19, 2021. It describes him as indicted in the Southern District of New York for fraud-related offenses, with no further resolution recorded in the list. The general warrant grants full pardons but does not explain why he was selected.
description_long: The Justice Department’s pardon list places Tommaso Buti under January 19, 2021, and identifies the Southern District of New York. It lists wire-fraud and money-laundering-related charges and describes the case as indicted with no further resolution recorded in the list. The public-disclosure link attached to the entry leads to an executive grant naming several pardon recipients, but the recovered document does not name Buti. The list therefore does not establish from the linked warrant what specific offenses the pardon covered. The sources suggest the pardon entry concerned an unresolved indictment rather than a prison sentence, but they do not establish the docket’s exact status on the date of the action. They also provide no person-specific explanation for selecting Buti. The case docket and an individual warrant or clemency statement are needed to confirm the scope and rationale; until then, the pardon record should remain qualified.

title: Commutes Sentence of David Morris Barren
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of David Morris Barren as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: The official warrant says Trump commuted David Morris Barren’s imprisonment on January 19, 2021, to time served. It left his five-year supervised-release term and all conditions intact; DOJ lists his original 30-year sentence, an earlier 2017 clemency change, and District of Maryland convictions in a drug and money-laundering case.
description_long: David Morris Barren’s commutation took effect through a January 19, 2021, executive warrant that changed his remaining prison term to time served. The warrant expressly left the court-imposed supervised-release term and its conditions, along with all other components of the sentence, in effect. The DOJ clemency list identifies a 30-year sentence in the District of Maryland, previously amended by executive clemency in 2017, followed by five years of supervised release. It lists a cocaine-distribution conspiracy and financial offenses including money laundering and structuring transactions. This was a commutation of imprisonment, not a pardon: it did not erase the convictions or cancel supervision and other sentence terms. The official warrant provides the new prison term and continuing release conditions that were missing from the earlier summary. The linked record does not give an individual explanation for the commutation, but the requested sentence outcome is documented in the warrant.

title: Commutes Sentence of Corvain T. Cooper
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Corvain T. Cooper as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: On January 19, 2021, the DOJ warrant commuted Corvain T. Cooper’s prison term to time served but kept his 10-year supervised-release term and all conditions intact. The linked clemency documents describe the sentence change but do not give a release date or explain why Trump selected Cooper for relief.
description_long: The Justice Department’s January 19, 2021, commutation warrant changed Corvain T. Cooper’s remaining prison sentence to time served. It explicitly left the court-imposed 10-year supervised-release term, its conditions, and all other sentence components in force. The DOJ clemency list identifies Cooper’s case in the Western District of North Carolina, with convictions for marijuana-trafficking conspiracy, money-laundering conspiracy, and structuring currency transactions. A commutation shortens the custody portion of a sentence but does not erase the convictions or cancel supervision. The warrant establishes the new prison term and continuing legal conditions, but it does not state the administration’s reason for granting relief or give a release date from a Bureau of Prisons facility. Those details are absent from the linked records, so this description records the documented legal effect without attributing a motive to Trump.
